title: How a CPU Works
subtitle: From one tiny instruction to billions per second.
objectives: Explain what the CPU does and why every computer needs one
Name the main CPU parts: ALU, control unit and registers
Describe the fetch, decode, execute cycle in the right order
Compare registers, cache, RAM and storage by speed and size
Trace a tiny program through the CPU, one instruction at a time

steps.question: Your phone plays music, runs a game and checks messages — all at once. How can one small chip do all that?
clues: A modern CPU runs **billions** of instructions every second.
Each instruction is tiny: add two numbers, copy a value, compare, jump.
So how do tiny steps become a whole game?

notes.explain: Let the class guess before you reveal anything. Do not give the answer yet: the whole lesson answers this question.
notes.ask: How many things do you think your phone does in one second?
notes.difficulty: Easy: this is a curiosity warm-up.

notes.explain: Read the five objectives aloud. Tell students they will check them off at the end in the learning report.

steps.title: The CPU executes instructions

items: A program is a long list of **instructions**.
The CPU runs them **one tiny step at a time**.
It does not understand — it follows instructions, extremely fast.

nodes.label: Input
nodes.note: Instructions and data arrive from memory.

nodes.label: Process
nodes.note: The CPU performs one tiny instruction at a time.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.note: Results go back to memory or out to a screen, speaker or network.

steps.why: Every app you use — games, browsers, AI — is millions of CPU instructions underneath.

explainAgain.beginner: Think of the CPU as a very fast worker with a to-do list. It reads one item, does it, then reads the next.
explainAgain.technical: The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction word from memory, decodes the opcode and operands, and executes the micro-operations that change registers or memory.
explainAgain.analogy: A cook following a recipe, one line at a time.

deeper.text: A real CPU can overlap instructions (a **pipeline**) and run several at once on different **cores**. We keep one-at-a-time for now.

notes.explain: Stress 'instructions are tiny'. The power comes from speed, not intelligence.
terms: **Instruction** — one small command the CPU can run
misconceptions: Students think the CPU 'thinks' or 'understands' code.
notes.ask: Is a CPU smart or fast?

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: Which job does the CPU do?
steps.why: The CPU's job is to execute instructions.
feedback: Storage (SSD or hard drive) keeps files. The CPU only works with data while it runs.
Pictures reach the screen through the display hardware (GPU). The CPU just sends it instructions.
Power comes from the power supply or battery, not the CPU.

steps.statement: A CPU understands your program the way a person would.
steps.why: It only follows simple instructions, very fast. It never 'understands' anything.

steps.title: Three parts do the work

nodes.label: ALU
nodes.note: The **Arithmetic Logic Unit** performs calculations and comparisons.

nodes.label: Control Unit
nodes.note: The **Control Unit** decodes each instruction and tells the other parts what to do.

nodes.label: Registers
nodes.note: **Registers** hold the few values the CPU is using right now.

steps.why: Knowing these parts lets you predict how fast a program can run and where it gets stuck.

explainAgain.beginner: Picture a kitchen. The **control unit** is the chef reading the recipe. The **ALU** is the chopping board where food is actually prepared. **Registers** are the small counter space holding what you are using now.

notes.explain: Click each box as you explain it. The note under the diagram changes with the highlighted part.
terms: **Register** — a tiny storage slot inside the CPU
**PC** — program counter, the address of the next instruction
misconceptions: The ALU does NOT decode instructions.

steps.title: How they cooperate

nodes.label: Control Unit
nodes.note: The control unit tells the registers which values to supply.

nodes.label: Registers
nodes.note: The two numbers to work on are placed on the ALU's inputs.

nodes.label: ALU
nodes.note: The ALU adds, subtracts or compares.

nodes.label: Registers
nodes.note: The answer is saved in a register for the next instruction.

steps.why: This tiny loop of control, data and calculation repeats for every instruction a program has.

steps.question: Which component performs arithmetic operations?
steps.why: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does maths and logic.
feedback: The control unit directs the other parts. It does not do the calculating.
Registers only hold values; they do not calculate.
Cache stores copies of data for speed. It does no arithmetic.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each component with its job.

pairs.b: Decodes instructions and directs the other parts
Hold the data being used right now
Remembers the address of the next instruction

steps.why: Each part has one clear job, and they work together.

questions.q: What is the job of the ALU?
questions.a: It performs arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic (compare, AND, OR).
They are the fastest storage, holding the values the CPU is working on right now.

questions.q: How is the control unit different from the ALU?
questions.a: The control unit decodes instructions and directs; the ALU does the calculating.

steps.title: Fetch, decode, execute

nodes.label: Fetch
nodes.note: The CPU reads the next instruction from memory, using the address in the **Program Counter**.

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.note: The **control unit** works out which operation is needed and which data it uses.

nodes.label: Execute
nodes.note: The **ALU** (or memory) performs the operation and the result is stored.

blocks.text: …then it **repeats**, billions of times every second.

steps.why: This one loop is behind everything your computer does, from a calculator to a video game.

explainAgain.beginner: Read a line of the recipe (fetch). Understand it (decode). Do it (execute). Then read the next line.
explainAgain.technical: The program counter supplies the address; the instruction register holds the fetched word; the control unit decodes it into control signals; the datapath executes it; the PC advances.

deeper.text: Modern CPUs overlap the three stages for different instructions at once. That is called **pipelining**, and it is how they sustain close to one instruction per clock cycle.

notes.explain: Play the flow once, then click each stage. Insist on the order.
misconceptions: Students swap decode and fetch: you cannot decode what you do not have yet.
notes.ask: What would happen if the CPU skipped the fetch step?

steps.question: A tiny program runs: `LOAD A, 5` then `ADD A, 3`. What will register A hold at the end?

steps.note: `LOAD A, 5` puts 5 into register A, so A = 5.
`ADD A, 3` adds 3 to A, so A = 5 + 3 = 8.

steps.result: Each instruction changes the registers a little. Together they build the answer.

steps.title: Trace a program

blocks.code:
LOAD A, 4
ADD A, 6
STORE A, [20]

steps.note: Cycle 1: fetch, decode, execute `LOAD`. A becomes 4.
Cycle 2: `ADD` runs in the ALU. A becomes 10.
Cycle 3: `STORE` copies A into memory address 20.

steps.why: Tracing by hand is how engineers find bugs, and how you will check your own understanding.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put the instruction cycle in the correct order.
items: Decode it to see what it means
steps.why: You cannot decode an instruction you have not fetched, and you cannot execute one you have not decoded.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why must the CPU **fetch** an instruction before it can decode it?
steps.answer: Decoding works on the instruction's bits, so the CPU must already have them. Fetching copies the instruction from memory into a register; only then can the control unit read it.

notes.explain: Let the timer run. Walk around; listen for the idea of 'you need it in hand first'.
notes.discuss: Does the CPU ever fetch the next instruction while still executing the last? (Yes: pipelining.)

steps.title: Memory: a study desk
steps.why: Programs feel slow when the CPU waits for data. Knowing the hierarchy tells you where the wait comes from.

explainAgain.beginner: The closer something is to your hands, the faster you can use it — but the less room there is. That is why computers keep a little of everything close, and the rest further away.

notes.explain: Use the 'Test me' button: hide the technical names and ask students to name them from the analogy.

steps.title: Faster means smaller

deeper.text: A register is read in under a nanosecond; RAM takes around 100 times longer; an SSD about 100,000 times longer. Caches exist to hide that gap.

steps.why: A faster CPU does not help if it is always waiting for slower memory.

steps.question: Why not make all memory as fast as registers?
options: It would be far too expensive and could not hold much
The CPU cannot use fast memory
steps.why: Very fast memory costs more and is physically small, so computers use a hierarchy of sizes and speeds.
steps.misconception: Speed is a trade-off with cost and capacity, not with reliability or compatibility.

steps.question: Name the three steps of the instruction cycle, in order.
steps.solution: The CPU fetches the instruction from memory, the control unit decodes it, and then the ALU or memory executes it. Then it repeats.

steps.question: Trace this program. What does A hold at the end, and how many instruction cycles ran?

code.code:
LOAD A, 7
ADD A, 5
ADD A, 2

steps.hint: Do one line at a time and write down A after each.
steps.solution:
Line 1: A = 7.
Line 2: A = 7 + 5 = 12.
Line 3: A = 12 + 2 = 14.
Three instructions means three fetch-decode-execute cycles.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One line below is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. The CPU fetches an instruction from memory.
steps.explain: Decoding is the control unit's job. The ALU only does arithmetic and logic.
steps.fix: The control unit decodes the instruction.

steps.question: A friend says: "My computer is slow, so I need a faster CPU." Their programs keep waiting for data from the hard drive. Is a faster CPU the best fix? Argue your answer using the memory hierarchy.
steps.hint: Where is the CPU spending its time?
steps.answer: Probably not. The CPU is idle, waiting for slow storage. Adding RAM or switching to an SSD removes that wait.
steps.solution: The slowest step controls total speed. A faster CPU just waits faster. Moving data closer (more RAM so less swapping, or an SSD instead of a hard drive) reduces the wait. A faster CPU only helps when the CPU, not memory, is the bottleneck.

steps.title: Final review
remember: ALU = maths, Control Unit = directs, Registers = tiny fast storage.
understand: The CPU is fast, not smart.
Faster memory is smaller and costs more.
The slowest part limits the whole system.
apply: Trace a short program by hand.
Explain why a faster CPU may not fix a slow computer.

mistakes.right: The control unit decodes; the ALU calculates.

mistakes.wrong: The CPU decodes before it fetches.
A faster CPU always makes a computer faster.
mistakes.right: If it waits for memory, it cannot.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: A CPU is a very fast instruction follower. The control unit decodes each instruction, the ALU calculates, and registers hold the values in use. This repeats in a fetch, decode, execute loop. Memory is arranged from small and fast (registers) to large and slow (storage), and the slowest part sets the pace.

questions.question: What does CPU stand for?
questions.why: CPU is short for Central Processing Unit.
questions.misconception: The C stands for Central: the CPU sits at the centre of the computer, processing instructions.

questions.statement: The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations.
questions.why: That is exactly the ALU's job.

questions.question: What is the first step of the instruction cycle?
questions.why: The instruction must be fetched before anything else can happen.
questions.misconception: Nothing can be decoded or executed until the instruction has been fetched from memory.

questions.question: Which component decodes instructions and tells the other parts what to do?
questions.why: The control unit decodes and directs.
questions.misconception: The ALU calculates and registers store values. Decoding and directing is the control unit's job.

questions.question: Which list goes from fastest to slowest?
questions.why: Registers are fastest, then cache, RAM and finally storage.
questions.misconception: Order by distance from the CPU: the closer the memory, the faster and smaller it is.

questions.question: After these instructions, what does A hold?
questions.misconception: Work one line at a time: LOAD sets A, then ADD adds to what A already holds.

questions.question: After the CPU fetches an instruction, what does the Program Counter normally point to?
options: The address of the next instruction
questions.why: The PC is advanced so the next fetch reads the following instruction.
questions.misconception: The PC does not hold results. It holds an address, and moves on so the next fetch finds the next instruction.

questions.question: Why do CPUs have a small cache instead of making all RAM that fast?
options: Very fast memory is expensive and small, so only a little is used
questions.why: Speed, cost and size trade off, so a small fast cache hides RAM's slowness.
questions.misconception: Cache is small because fast memory is costly and takes up chip space. It is not about forgetting or compatibility.

questions.question: How many instruction cycles run, and what is A at the end?

code.code:
LOAD A, 3
ADD A, 4
ADD A, A

questions.why: Three instructions give three cycles. A = 3, then 7, then 7 + 7 = 14.
questions.misconception: Count each instruction as one cycle, then update A line by line. Remember the last line adds A to itself.

items.q: What is the job of the CPU?
items.a: To execute instructions, one tiny step at a time.

items.q: What are the three steps of the instruction cycle?
What is the difference between the ALU and the control unit?
items.a: The ALU calculates; the control unit decodes and directs.

items.q: Why is memory arranged in levels?
items.a: Faster memory is smaller and costs more, so a hierarchy gives speed and capacity together.
